Suggestions:

1) Don't complain about other people's plays--it's their choice, not yours.  Just because it's not the play you would have made doesn't make it any less valid or desirable.  Yeah, we're gonna take some damage this round--that's fine.  We're not going to die and we're not going to lose the game because of that.  And, even if we do?  No big loss.  It's a game.  Shuffle the cards, choose a new villain, and we play again.  No big whoop.

5) Making yourself out to sound like an "expert" in a game that, by your own admission, you've only played a limited number of times (and rarely with others) is beyond egotistical.  There are people on this board who have been playing this game since before the original edition was released--don't pretend to act like you know the game better than them.  That's the attitude you're conveying and it rubs people the wrong way--(see also: the Argent Adept discussion elsewhere on the board, where you admit to not understanding or liking AA, then want to write an instructional guide on how he works).

PlatinumWarlock:

Don't complain about other people's plays–it's their choice, not yours.  Just because it's not the play you would have made doesn't make it any less valid or desirable.



True, but this game is a team effort, so some collaboration should be occurring.  Tachyon is close to dead, and none of us is looking to sprightly; I am firmly of the opinion that we needed that Ground Pound.  Plus it was kind of a waste of the extremely powerful, game-ending Haka of Battle to add just 1 damage on a villain who's still above half (if we desperately needed to finish off a Drone or something, that'd be different of course).  I didn't mean to come across as telling anyone what they have to do, but rather what they should do, for the sake of the group.  Though I confess that from my perspective, the distinction between "you have no choice but to do this" and "you have a choice, but one choice is obviously right and the other is obviously wrong, so we're trusting you to do what we're all counting on you to decide to" is less than dramatic; I really don't get why so many people make such a big deal about it, but I suspect the answer is related to emotions, which I don't understand very well (my own least of all).

Yeah, we're gonna take some damage this round–that's fine.  We're not going to die and we're not going to lose the game because of that.


Dropship Omnitron adds +1 to all damage, and could potentially put out six more drones this turn and then fire a Flechettes (I counted, not that I really had to, being extremely familiar with Omnitron's deck in particular).  Yes, we very easily could lose heroes or even the game because of a one-turn lapse in our protection, particularly in a violent environment like Silver Gulch, with the most damaging of its cards already in play.


And, even if we do?  No big loss.  It's a game.  Shuffle the cards, choose a new villain, and we play again.  No big whoop.


This would be the point we disagree on.  While I don't want victory to be a foregone conclusion, I do think it's of critical importance to try for it within the context of a coop game, or else the experience becomes gratuitous and meaningless.  I don't see any point in playing at all if you're not going to take it seriously, at least not over the Internet (in person might be a more relaxed atmosphere, though I would probably still look askance at my fellow players if they didn't seem to care whether they got their own character killed, let alone mine).  Gaming is Serious Business in my world; it's my passion, it's my vocation, it's something I dedicate myself to with an almost psychotic intensity, and I'm sorry if that means a few people get rubbed the wrong way.


2) Handle your own Hero and go from there.  This is why I said, earlier, to not try to recreate the whole game on your own.


I can't possibly visualize the game state without having the components to look at.  I know there are people who can play chess in their head just by calling out moves, but my brain doesn't have such potent software.  I need scratch paper to do math, and I need a table to set up a game upon.  Once I can see the entire picture, that's when my brain starts spotting the patterns and connections, and I become aware of every tiniest detail.  (As an aside, this is also what makes me good at my job.  When I have one.)


Case in point, there was no talk of using External Combustion this round, so several people focused on drones.


I did not have an opportunity to ask whether you wanted me to play XC, nor to mention that I was hoping Haka would Ground-Pound…you all posted while I was asleep, or maybe it was while I was out buying groceries.  The key to a coop game is for the players to coordinate their activities, and when we're not all in a room able to talk to each other, that becomes more difficult.  I didn't really see you guys focusing on drones to any great extent (you hit them with multi-target attacks, and the only other places those could have gone was to Tyler Hayes, which might have been wiser but not so much so as to be obvious), but if you were counting on me to play XC this round, all you had to do was ask.  Since you got rid of the dangerous drone, there was no longer any real need, so I chose to set up for next turn, but if anyone had asked me to do otherwise, I would have at least considered their input.  


Telling someone "hey, you counted your damage wrong" is fine, but don't be condescending or rude about it.


Again, I do apologize that the distinction between rude and non-rude is largely invisible to me.  I shall endeavor to tread with greater caution.  My mind is a lot like Bunker's armor - massive and powerful, capable of crushing fragile objects that get in the way.  I did not mean to bruise any egos, and I am regretful that I am not better at managing my responsibility to avoid this.


Making yourself out to sound like an "expert" in a game that, by your own admission, you've only played a limited number of times (and rarely with others) is beyond egotistical.


I never said I was an expert…I only said that I play perfectly (which is true or very nearly so, within the context of having a day or so to analyze the board between turns; I screw up quite frequently in my solitaire games, because I have too much work to doo in too much of a hurry).  Like the data entry work I do with spectacularly high accuracy, this does not require knowledge, only an intense focus on fine details, and that state comes quite naturally to me.  It makes me extremely well qualified to keep track of all the fine details that others think are too much for anyone to have to manage.  It's not necessarily true that my tactics are perfect or anything, only that I notice things that others may have missed, and wish to point them out, so that everyone fully understands the truth which only I seem able to perceive.


(see also: the Argent Adept discussion elsewhere on the board, where you admit to not understanding or liking AA, then want to write an instructional guide on how he works).


One, my saying I didn't like or understand him was weeks before my saying I wanted to write a guide about him…I played him several times in the interim and began to comprehend how he functions.  And two, part of the point of my wanting to write a guide (which I have in fact started doing) was to help me understand him better, and I'm not the first person on these boards to use that logic.  Sometimes you have to go through the steps of a process in order to understand where it leads.
